topic: Day 1 · Renal Replacement Therapy — Indications, Modalities & Timing
speakerTitle: Consultant in Nephrology & Intensive Care Medicine
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Renal & Critical Care Units
speakerBio: Nephrologist-intensivist who leads the hospital's acute dialysis service and teaches that the hardest question in RRT is never 'how' but 'whether and when' — and that the timing trials should have retired the reflex to start early.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 52-year-old man with AKI on a background of sepsis has a potassium of 7.1 mmol/L with peaked T waves and a widening QRS on the monitor, a pH of 7.10, and an oxygen requirement rising from pulmonary oedema he can no longer diurese. The medical registrar has already given calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose and salbutamol — twice — and the potassium is still 6.8. The bed manager asks whether he "really needs the renal team overnight or can it wait till the morning ward round." This is the moment every acute physician must be able to recognise cold: some of these numbers are emergency indications for renal-replacement therapy, and the decision to dialyse is not a nephrology nicety — it is resuscitation. This session is about knowing exactly when RRT is life-saving, which modality to choose, and — the harder, evidence-rich question — when to start it.

1 · 🚨 Emergency indications — AEIOU

Renal-replacement therapy in AKI has a small number of absolute, life-threatening indications that override any timing debate. When one of these is present and refractory to medical therapy, you dialyse — now. The mnemonic is AEIOU:

LetterIndicationThe refractory threshold that triggers RRT
A — AcidosisSevere metabolic acidosispH < ~7.1 (or <7.15) not correctable medically, especially with volume constraints on bicarbonate
E — ElectrolytesRefractory hyperkalaemiaK⁺ > ~6.5 (or rising/with ECG changes) not responding to medical treatment
I — IntoxicationsDialysable poisonsToxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol), salicylates, lithium, metformin-associated lactic acidosis
O — OverloadFluid overload / pulmonary oedemaDiuretic-resistant volume overload compromising oxygenation
U — UraemiaUraemic complicationsUraemic pericarditis, uraemic encephalopathy, unexplained uraemic bleeding
AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolytes, Intoxications, Overload, Uraemia. A refractory member of this list is a same-hour dialysis decision — not a morning-ward-round decision.
💡 SLED / SLED the poisons you can dialyse

Not every poison is dialysable — dialysability needs a low molecular weight, low protein binding, small volume of distribution and water solubility. The classic removable toxins: methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate, lithium, and metformin (via its lactic acidosis). Highly protein-bound or large-volume-of-distribution drugs (e.g. tricyclics, digoxin) are not effectively cleared — reaching for dialysis there wastes time. Know the list before the toxicology emergency arrives.

⚠️ Uraemic pericarditis is a dialyse-today emergency

A pericardial friction rub in an advanced-AKI/uraemic patient is not a benign sign — uraemic pericarditis can progress to haemorrhagic effusion and tamponade, and it is an unequivocal indication for urgent RRT. Note the trap: therapeutic anticoagulation (including heparin during dialysis) can precipitate haemorrhagic transformation, so uraemic pericarditis is one of the strongest arguments for heparin-free or regional citrate anticoagulation on the circuit.

2 · ⚙️ The modalities — IHD vs CRRT vs SLED

Once you have decided to dialyse, you choose how. The three broad options trade speed of clearance against haemodynamic tolerability. The physiological principle: rapid solute and fluid removal causes rapid osmotic and volume shifts, which an unstable, vasopressor-dependent patient tolerates poorly.

FeatureIntermittent HD (IHD)Continuous RRT (CVVH / CVVHDF)SLED / hybrid
Duration3–5 hours, intermittentContinuous (24 h/day)~6–12 hours (extended)
Clearance speedFastSlow, gradualIntermediate
Haemodynamic tolerancePoorer — rapid shifts drop BPBest — gentle, ideal for shocked/pressor-dependent patientsGood — a middle ground
Fluid removalLarge volumes fast (good for flash overload if tolerated)Precise, gradual, hour-by-hourSteady
Anticoagulation needLess circuit timeContinuous circuit → citrate/heparin neededIntermediate
Mobility / logisticsFrees the patient between sessions; needs a dialysis nurseTies patient to the machine; ICU-basedFits a working shift; less machine time
Best forHaemodynamically stable; urgent hyperK/poison clearance; ward or unitShocked, pressor-dependent, raised ICP, cerebral oedemaImproving/intermediate patients, resource-limited units
🎯 CRRT modes decoded — diffusion vs convection

CVVH (haemofiltration) clears solute by convection — dragging solute across the membrane with a large volume of ultrafiltrate ("solvent drag"), better for larger 'middle molecules'. CVVHD (haemodialysis) clears by diffusion down a concentration gradient using countercurrent dialysate, better for small solutes. CVVHDF combines both. For most AKI the choice between CVVH and CVVHDF makes little outcome difference; what matters clinically is the continuous, gentle nature versus intermittent. Importantly, no modality has been shown to improve survival over another — CRVT vs IHD is a choice about tolerability and logistics, not mortality.

Continuous therapy is gentler, not more curative. Choose CRRT for the shocked, pressor-dependent patient because it removes fluid and solute slowly — not because it saves more lives than IHD. It doesn't.

3 · ⏱️ The timing debate — earlier is NOT better

Here is the single most important evidence lesson in acute nephrology of the last decade. For years, intuition said "start dialysis early, before the patient is uraemic and overloaded — get ahead of it." A run of large randomised trials demolished that intuition for the patient without an emergency indication.

TrialDesignResult
ELAIN (2016)Single-centre, mostly surgical; early vs delayedSuggested a mortality benefit to earlier start — the outlier, single-centre, hypothesis-generating
AKIKI (2016)Multicentre; early vs delayed (wait for a hard indication)No survival difference; ~half the delayed group never needed RRT at all
IDEAL-ICU (2018)Septic shock with AKI; early vs delayedNo difference in 90-day mortality; stopped for futility
STARRT-AKI (2020)The definitive ~3,000-patient multinational trial; accelerated vs standardNo mortality benefit to accelerated start; accelerated arm had more dependence on dialysis at 90 days and more adverse events (hypotension, hypophosphataemia, line complications)
🎯 What the timing trials actually teach

In a patient without an emergency (AEIOU) indication, routine early initiation of RRT does not improve survival and may cause harm — more line and circuit complications, more hypotension, and a higher chance of remaining dialysis-dependent — while a watchful-waiting strategy lets a substantial fraction of patients recover renal function and avoid dialysis entirely. The modern approach: dialyse promptly for a genuine AEIOU emergency, and otherwise watch and wait, monitoring closely, resisting the urge to start 'to get ahead of it'. Start for a reason, not for a number.

STARRT-AKI, AKIKI and IDEAL-ICU: earlier routine dialysis does not save lives, and waiting lets many kidneys recover without ever needing it. Start RRT for an emergency indication, not a creatinine threshold.

4 · 💊 Dose — how much clearance

Dose in CRRT is prescribed as effluent flow rate in mL/kg/hour. The landmark ATN (VA/NIH, 2008) and RENAL (2009) trials compared intensive versus less-intensive dosing and found no benefit to higher-intensity RRT. KDIGO therefore recommends a delivered effluent dose of 20–25 mL/kg/h for CRRT (and Kt/V ~3.9/week for intermittent).

  • Prescribe higher than target because delivered dose is always less than prescribed — downtime for clotting, filter changes, imaging, and procedures erodes it. Prescribe ~25–30 to deliver 20–25.
  • More is not better: higher-intensity RRT gives no survival benefit and increases removal of nutrients, phosphate, antibiotics and other drugs — worsening hypophosphataemia and risking antimicrobial under-dosing.
⚠️ RRT strips antibiotics and phosphate — dose around it

Continuous RRT clears many antibiotics (β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides) — under-dosing on the circuit risks treatment failure in the very septic patient who needs source control. Always dose antimicrobials for the patient's RRT modality with pharmacy input. RRT also removes phosphate and causes hypophosphataemia (an under-recognised cause of failure to wean from the ventilator and of muscle weakness) — monitor and replace, sometimes by adding phosphate to the dialysate.

5 · 🩸 Anticoagulation — regional citrate vs heparin

A continuous extracorporeal circuit clots without anticoagulation, wasting filters and blood. The two main strategies:

Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA)Systemic heparin
MechanismCitrate chelates ionised calcium in the circuit → no clotting in the filter; calcium reinfused to the patient → no systemic anticoagulationSystemic unfractionated heparin anticoagulates the whole patient
Bleeding riskLower — anticoagulation confined to the circuitHigher — systemic
Filter lifeLongerShorter
Main hazardCitrate accumulation (esp. hepatic failure/shock) → metabolic acidosis, high total-to-ionised calcium ratio; also hypocalcaemia/alkalosisBleeding; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
Guideline stanceKDIGO-preferred first-line where no contraindicationReserve where citrate contraindicated or unavailable
KDIGO prefers regional citrate anticoagulation over heparin for CRRT — it keeps the anticoagulation in the circuit, prolongs filter life and lowers bleeding. Watch for citrate accumulation in the patient with a failing liver.
💡 Reading citrate accumulation

Citrate is normally metabolised to bicarbonate by the liver. In hepatic failure or severe shock it accumulates: it chelates systemic calcium, giving a rising total calcium with a falling ionised calcium — a total:ionised calcium ratio > 2.5 is the classic warning — plus a worsening metabolic acidosis. The fix is to reduce or stop the citrate. In the uraemic-pericarditis or high-bleeding-risk patient who also cannot tolerate citrate, run the circuit heparin-free with frequent saline flushes.

6 · 🔌 Vascular access & when to stop

Vascular access

  • Acute RRT uses a large-bore, dual-lumen, non-tunnelled central dialysis catheter (a "vascath"). Preferred site order (per KDIGO): right internal jugular > femoral > left internal jugular > subclavian last.
  • Avoid the subclavian where possible — subclavian stenosis jeopardises future permanent arteriovenous fistula formation in a patient who may progress to chronic dialysis.
  • Insert under ultrasound guidance; a poorly-functioning line (inadequate flows, recirculation) is the commonest cause of poor delivered dose and circuit clotting.

When to stop

  • Recovering renal function is the signal to wean — a rising spontaneous urine output is the best practical bedside marker that native kidneys are returning; a falling creatinine while off/between sessions, and improving clearance, support stopping.
  • Stop when the emergency indication has resolved and the kidney is doing enough work itself. There is no need to continue RRT to an arbitrary creatinine target once the patient is recovering.
  • Deciding to stop is as evidence-thin as deciding to start — use trajectory (urine output, metabolic control off support) rather than a single number.

7 · 🧑‍⚕️ M&M — the heparin that bled the pericardium

☠️ Mortality & Morbidity — anticoagulation in the wrong patient

A 60-year-old man with advanced AKI developed a pericardial friction rub and a small effusion — uraemic pericarditis, a clear emergency indication for RRT. He was started on intermittent haemodialysis with systemic heparin as the default circuit anticoagulant, because "that's what we always use." Over the next twelve hours his effusion enlarged and became haemorrhagic; he developed cardiac tamponade — hypotension, a rising JVP, pulsus paradoxus — and required emergency pericardiocentesis. Lessons: (1) uraemic pericarditis inflames the pericardium and systemic anticoagulation can precipitate haemorrhagic transformation and tamponade — it is a specific contraindication to heparin on the circuit; (2) the correct choice was regional citrate (or heparin-free dialysis with saline flushes), keeping anticoagulation out of the patient; (3) 'that's what we always use' is not an anticoagulation strategy — the circuit anticoagulant must be chosen for the individual patient's bleeding risk and liver function. He survived, but a foreseeable tamponade was created by defaulting to systemic heparin in the one patient in whom it was most dangerous.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Emergency indications = AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolytes (refractory hyperkalaemia), Intoxications, Overload, Uraemia (pericarditis/encephalopathy). A refractory member is a same-hour dialysis decision.
  2. Modality trades speed for tolerance: IHD is fast but haemodynamically harsh; CRRT (CVVH/CVVHDF) is gentle and best for the shocked, pressor-dependent patient; SLED is the hybrid middle ground. No modality improves survival over another.
  3. Earlier routine initiation does NOT save lives (STARRT-AKI, AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU) and may harm; watchful waiting lets many kidneys recover and avoid dialysis. Start for an AEIOU reason, not a creatinine number.
  4. Dose: effluent 20–25 mL/kg/h (RENAL, ATN — higher intensity gives no benefit); prescribe higher to deliver target, and dose antibiotics/phosphate around the clearance.
  5. Regional citrate is KDIGO-preferred anticoagulation over heparin — circuit-confined, longer filter life, less bleeding; watch for citrate accumulation (total:ionised Ca >2.5) in liver failure.
  6. Access: non-tunnelled dual-lumen vascath, ultrasound-guided, right IJ > femoral > left IJ > avoid subclavian (protect future fistula sites).
  7. Stop RRT on recovery — a rising spontaneous urine output is the best bedside marker that native kidneys are returning.

moderatorQs.q: A patient with AKI has a potassium of 6.9 with ECG changes, unresponsive to two rounds of medical therapy. Walk me through why this is an RRT decision and what else in the AEIOU list you'd screen for.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Refractory hyperkalaemia is the 'E' of AEIOU and, when it is not responding to medical treatment (calcium for membrane stabilisation, insulin-dextrose and salbutamol to shift potassium, and attempts at removal), it is an emergency indication for RRT — because the next event is a malignant arrhythmia or arrest. This is a same-hour dialysis decision that overrides any timing debate. Having identified it, I would screen the rest of AEIOU: Acidosis (a pH below ~7.1 not medically correctable), Intoxications (a dialysable poison — methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate, lithium, metformin-associated lactic acidosis), Overload (diuretic-resistant pulmonary oedema compromising oxygenation), and Uraemia (pericarditis or encephalopathy). Any refractory member confirms the need and the urgency.

moderatorQs.q: Summarise what STARRT-AKI, AKIKI and IDEAL-ICU changed about when we start dialysis in AKI.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: They dismantled the intuition that starting dialysis early — before overt uraemia or overload — improves outcomes. AKIKI and IDEAL-ICU (the latter in septic shock) found no survival difference between early and delayed strategies, and in AKIKI roughly half the delayed group never needed RRT at all because their kidneys recovered. STARRT-AKI, the definitive ~3,000-patient trial, confirmed no mortality benefit to an accelerated start and showed the accelerated arm had more dependence on dialysis at 90 days and more adverse events. The practice change: in a patient without an emergency (AEIOU) indication, adopt a watchful-waiting strategy — monitor closely and start only for a genuine indication — rather than initiating routinely 'to get ahead of it'. Start for a reason, not for a number. (ELAIN, a single-centre surgical trial, suggested early benefit but is the outlier.)

moderatorQs.q: Why does KDIGO prefer regional citrate anticoagulation over heparin for continuous RRT, and what is the danger you must watch for?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) confines anticoagulation to the extracorporeal circuit: citrate chelates ionised calcium in the filter to prevent clotting, and calcium is reinfused to the patient so there is no systemic anticoagulation. Compared with systemic heparin this gives longer filter life and a lower bleeding risk, and it avoids heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — hence KDIGO's preference where there is no contraindication. The danger to watch for is citrate accumulation, mainly in hepatic failure or severe shock where citrate is not metabolised to bicarbonate: it chelates systemic calcium, producing a rising total calcium with a falling ionised calcium — a total:ionised calcium ratio > 2.5 is the classic warning — plus a worsening metabolic acidosis. The response is to reduce or stop the citrate.

audienceQs.q: My patient is in septic shock on noradrenaline and needs RRT. Should I use intermittent haemodialysis or CRRT, and does it affect survival?
audienceQs.answerHTML: For a shocked, vasopressor-dependent patient, choose continuous RRT (CVVH or CVVHDF). Intermittent haemodialysis removes fluid and solute rapidly, causing osmotic and volume shifts that an unstable patient tolerates poorly — dropping the blood pressure and worsening pressor requirements. CRRT removes fluid and solute slowly and precisely, which is far gentler haemodynamically, and it is also preferred where there is raised intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema. Crucially, though, this is a choice about tolerability and logistics, not mortality — no modality has been shown to improve survival over another. So use CRRT here because your patient will tolerate it better, and plan to step down to SLED or intermittent HD as they stabilise.

audienceQs.q: What should I be adjusting on the drug chart once a patient starts continuous RRT?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Two big things. First, antibiotics: CRRT clears many antimicrobials — β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides — so doses must be adjusted up to the RRT-specific regimen to avoid under-dosing the septic patient, which risks treatment failure. Don't apply standard 'renal impairment' reductions on CRRT; use CRRT-specific dosing. Second, watch and replace phosphate — CRRT removes it and hypophosphataemia is a common, under-recognised cause of muscle weakness and failure to wean from the ventilator (some units add phosphate to the dialysate). More broadly, remember the effluent dose target is only 20–25 mL/kg/h — higher intensity gives no benefit and strips more drugs and nutrients — and review all renally-cleared drugs and any nephrotoxins for the new clearance.

audienceQs.q: How do we know when it's time to stop dialysis in someone who's recovering?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The single most useful bedside signal is a rising spontaneous urine output — it is the best practical marker that the native kidneys are coming back online. Alongside that, you look for improving clearance and a falling creatinine while off or between sessions, and resolution of whatever emergency indication (hyperkalaemia, acidosis, overload, uraemia) prompted RRT in the first place. Once the kidney is doing enough work itself and the metabolic parameters hold up off support, you can wean and stop — there's no need to continue to an arbitrary creatinine target. Like the decision to start, the decision to stop is guided by trajectory rather than a single number, so we trend urine output and metabolic control rather than waiting for one 'normal' result.
